title: Points of controversy
hook: a book of debates with other early schools, set out question and answer

segments.voice: Yesterday, strong support: weather, food, people and places leaning hard on the mind. Your line: good supports. Which support did you choose on purpose? Day one thousand ninety.

Is the person known as a real and ultimate fact? Yes. Then is the person known in the same way as other real and ultimate facts? No, that can't be said. Then your first answer needs another look. That's roughly how one book of the Abhidhamma begins: not with a list, but with an argument. Two voices, back and forth, about whether there is a person beyond the parts. It reads less like a lecture than a transcript of a very patient debate club. Today, the book of debates.
screen: `IS THE PERSON REAL?` → `YES. THEN IN THE SAME WAY?` → `A BOOK THAT ARGUES.`

segments.voice: The book is the Kathavatthu, usually translated points of controversy. It's one of the books of the Theravada Abhidhamma, and tradition says an elder named Moggaliputta Tissa set it out to answer views held by other early Buddhist schools. Its method is the surprise. Each debate starts with a question to the other side. The other side answers. Then the questioner follows the answer to its consequences, step by step, until a tension shows: if you say this, then you must also say that, and you have already said you won't. The other side gets to push back, and in places it cites the Buddha's own words in its support. The book doesn't name the schools it debates; the later commentary does that work. The first debate is about the person. One group of early Buddhists, known as the personalists, held that there is a person who is neither the same as the body and mind nor separate from them, and they pointed to places where the Buddha speaks of a person. The Kathavatthu's side answers that such talk is a way of speaking, true in its place, but not one more ultimate thing beside matter and mind. Both sides were Buddhists, reading the same teacher closely and arriving at different answers. The book keeps going through many more questions: whether an awakened person can fall back, whether past and future things exist. What's worth taking home isn't who won. It's the form. Write the other side's answer down in its own words. Follow it honestly. Let them reply.
screen: `QUESTION, ANSWER, CONSEQUENCE.` · `THE OTHER SIDE CITES THE BUDDHA TOO.` · `THE FIRST DEBATE: THE PERSON.` · then, large: `BOTH SIDES, READING ONE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: hear one opposing point fully. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a view you disagree with, something small or something big. Now, quietly, let it speak in its own words, the way someone who holds it would say it, at its best. Don't answer it yet. Notice what in you wants to interrupt. Let that settle, and hear the point out to its end. Then rest with the breath. You don't have to agree. The bell holds the time.
Kathavatthu. Points of controversy: a book of the Abhidhamma set out as question and answer with other early schools, beginning with the person. Today's word.

Your line: points of controversy. Today, in one disagreement, say the other person's point back in their words before you give your own, and see whether they agree you heard it. Day one thousand ninety.

howItsDone: Theravada scholars study the Kathavatthu as part of the Abhidhamma, with its commentary naming the schools behind each view, and monastic debate and question-and-answer study continue in several Buddhist traditions.

original.note: Pali: points of discussion or controversy; a book of the Theravada Abhidhamma set out as debate.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient book that tells you who was right.
what it means: a record of Buddhists debating Buddhists, question, answer and consequence, both sides citing the same teacher.
what a scholar hears: the Kathavatthu, attributed by tradition to Moggaliputta Tissa; its opponents are unnamed in the text and identified by the commentary.
recall: the awakened one, a title, not a name

sources.ref: Kathavatthu I.1 (the debate on the person)

notes: The hook's opening exchange paraphrases the start of Kathavatthu I.1 (Shwe Zan Aung and C. A. F. Rhys Davids' Points of Controversy renders it with 'the soul'/'person'); not quoted. Confirm the paraphrase.
'The first debate is about the person' (Kathavatthu I.1); a claim that it is also the longest was cut under the claims rule.
Moggaliputta Tissa's authorship is given as 'tradition says'; the third council setting and Ashoka are left out under the claims rule.
The personalists (Pudgalavada: Vatsiputriya, Sammitiya) described as holding a person neither identical to nor different from the aggregates; confirm the framing is fair to them.
'In places it cites the Buddha's own words': the opponent cites sutta passages speaking of a person (e.g. the person who works for his own welfare). Confirm.
Topics named: falling back of an arahant (I.2) and whether past and future exist (I.6, the 'all exists' debate); confirm.
howItsDone mentions monastic debate in 'several Buddhist traditions' (e.g. Tibetan debate); soften if needed.
